title: Software Development
blurb: Work as a team from requirements to delivery, and understand what “done” means.

mustKnow.title: SDLC and Agile / Scrum in practice
mustKnow.body: SDLC is the cycle of planning → design → development → testing → delivery → maintenance. Agile does not eliminate these stages; it completes the cycle in short iterations to get feedback on working software as early as possible. In Scrum (Scrum Guide 2020), each Sprint lasts at most one month, has a clear Sprint Goal, and uses Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective to inspect and adapt. A common trap is holding every ceremony without changing anything based on the Review or Retrospective: waterfall cut into pieces.

mustKnow.title: User stories: who, what, and why
mustKnow.body: A user story describes a need from the user’s perspective: “As a… I want… so that…”. The “so that” matters most because it identifies the actual problem and allows the team to suggest a simpler solution. A story starts a conversation rather than serving as a complete specification. Use INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) to check its quality. A common trap is attaching “As a developer” to technical tasks without explaining their value to users.

mustKnow.title: Acceptance criteria with Given / When / Then
mustKnow.body: Acceptance criteria are the conditions that must hold for a story to be accepted as complete. Given describes the starting state, When the action, and Then an observable, verifiable result. Write them before implementation through a conversation between the PO, developers, and QA to reveal misunderstandings early; they can often translate almost directly into automated tests. Include failure cases, such as an expired link, rather than only the happy path.
mustKnow.code:
As a customer, I want to reset my password by email
so that I can regain access to my account if I forget it.

Given a customer has an account with a verified email address
When they select “Forgot password” and enter that email address
Then they receive an email with a reset link valid for 30 minutes

Given a reset link was created more than 30 minutes ago
When the customer opens it
Then they see an expired-link message and can request a new link

mustKnow.title: Measurable functional and non-functional requirements
mustKnow.body: Functional requirements describe what a system does, such as allowing users to add products to a cart. Non-functional requirements (NFRs) describe how well it must do it: performance, security, availability, or accessibility. Make NFRs verifiable, usually with numbers and conditions, such as “The API responds within 300 ms at p95 under 500 requests per second”; p95 means 95% of requests are faster than this value. Avoid vague statements such as “fast” or “supports many users”. Some requirements need no numeric threshold, such as requiring TLS for communication. Unwritten NFRs are often discovered during production outages, when fixing them costs the most.

mustKnow.title: Definition of Done
mustKnow.body: The Definition of Done (DoD) is the team’s shared quality standard that every item must meet to count as done. Acceptance criteria, by contrast, belong to individual stories. Under the Scrum Guide 2020, work that does not meet the DoD cannot be presented at the Sprint Review or released, and must return to the Product Backlog. Accepting work as “90% done” hides unfinished work and makes velocity misleading.
mustKnow.code:
- [ ] All acceptance criteria pass
- [ ] Automated tests exist and CI passes
- [ ] At least one reviewer has completed code review
- [ ] Deployed to staging and verified
- [ ] Relevant documentation / changelog updated

mustKnow.title: Code review that helps
mustKnow.body: Review aims to improve overall code health and spread knowledge, rather than catch people out or wait for perfection. Respond quickly: Google’s guidance says each response to a review request should take no more than one business day. Focus on correctness, security, design, and tests, leaving style to formatters or linters. Useful comments identify the problem, explain why it matters, and offer alternatives. Label their importance: “Nit:” marks a small issue that technically should be addressed but has little impact; Google treats it as polish the author may omit if it is not important enough to hold up the PR. Use “Optional/Consider” for truly optional suggestions. Authors help by submitting small PRs explaining what changed, why, and how it was tested.

mustKnow.title: Split work into vertical slices
mustKnow.body: Break large stories into thin slices that cross every layer (UI → API → database) and each deliver usable value. Splitting by technical layer leaves nothing usable until all pieces are complete. Slices that can finish in one or two days provide fast feedback, smaller PRs, and visible progress. Common approaches split by workflow step, business rule, or channel, or deliver the happy path before adding special cases.
mustKnow.code:
Large story: support all payment methods

Split by layer (no piece is usable on its own):
  DB tables → API → UI

Vertical slices (each piece can be delivered):
  1. Successful credit card payment, end to end
  2. Show a message when a card is declined
  3. Add PromptPay QR payments
  4. Add installment payments

mustKnow.title: Estimate honestly
mustKnow.body: An estimate is an uncertain prediction, not a promise. Give a range, such as three to five days, along with known assumptions and risks. For completely unknown areas, run a short, time-boxed spike to reduce uncertainty first. Story points compare relative size within a team and cannot be compared across teams. Do not lower estimates just to please the person asking; when you know delivery will be late, communicate promptly with alternatives such as reducing scope.

mustKnow.title: Technical debt
mustKnow.body: Technical debt consists of shortcuts or designs that no longer fit, slowing subsequent changes like interest payments; Ward Cunningham used the metaphor in 1992. Some debt can be taken deliberately to ship on time if it is recorded with a repayment plan. Make it visible in the backlog with measurable effects, such as “Changes to this module take twice as long”, and repay it regularly, starting with the most frequently changed areas. Rewriting the entire system at once is often riskier and slower than expected.

mustKnow.title: ADRs: record why a decision was made
mustKnow.body: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short document, one file per important decision, stored alongside code in the repository. Michael Nygard’s popular format includes Title, Status, Context, Decision, and Consequences. It preserves the reasons and context for future team members, avoiding repeated debates. Do not rewrite an accepted ADR retrospectively; when the decision changes, create a new ADR and mark the old one superseded.
mustKnow.code:
# ADR-007: Use PostgreSQL as the primary database
Status: Accepted

## Context
Order data has complex relationships and requires transactions.

## Decision
Use PostgreSQL instead of MongoDB.

## Consequences
+ ACID transactions and JOINs
- Schema migrations must be planned for every structural change

mustKnow.title: Forecast from data: cycle time and throughput
mustKnow.body: Use the team’s actual delivery data instead of guessing: cycle time is the time from starting to finishing each item, and throughput is the number of items completed per week. Little’s Law says that in a reasonably stable system, average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput. If throughput does not fall, reducing WIP shortens average cycle time; the equation concerns averages and does not guarantee the duration of every item. Historical throughput can support Monte Carlo simulations giving probabilities, such as “an 85% chance of completing 40 items within six weeks”, which is more honest than a single number.

mustKnow.title: Outcomes matter more than outputs
mustKnow.body: Outputs are what a team produces, such as feature counts or story points. Outcomes are actual benefits for users and the business, such as higher conversion, less user effort, or fewer tickets. Shipping many features without improving anything wastes effort. Set measurable outcome goals, hypothesize which metric a feature will affect, and measure after release to choose what to work on next. Velocity can support planning within a team but does not measure success.

mustKnow.title: The Agile Manifesto: four values and 12 principles
mustKnow.body: The Agile Manifesto (2001) values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. It explicitly says the items on the right still have value, so it does not remove the need for documentation or plans. The 12 principles expand these values, including frequent delivery of working software, welcoming changing requirements even late in development, and treating working software as the primary measure of progress. A common trap is invoking the Manifesto to stop planning or documenting.

mustKnow.title: Scrum: three accountabilities and artifact commitments
mustKnow.body: The Scrum Guide 2020 defines three accountabilities in a Scrum Team: Developers plan the Sprint Backlog, maintain quality through the Definition of Done, and adapt their plan daily toward the Sprint Goal; the Product Owner maximizes product value and manages the Product Backlog, including ordering its items; and the Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Guide and for team effectiveness. Each artifact has a commitment: Product Backlog → Product Goal, Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal, and Increment → Definition of Done. The Product Owner is one person, not a committee; anyone seeking Backlog changes must persuade the PO. A common trap is treating the Scrum Master as a manager who assigns tasks, although the Guide leaves the method of turning items into an Increment to the Developers.

mustKnow.title: Semantic Versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
mustKnow.body: Semantic Versioning uses MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH to communicate upgrade impact. Increase MAJOR for incompatible public API changes, MINOR for compatible functionality additions and declared deprecations, and PATCH for compatible bug fixes. Increasing a component resets components to its right to zero. Version 0.y.z is initial development, when anything may change. A pre-release such as 1.0.0-rc.1 ranks below 1.0.0, and build metadata after + is ignored when comparing precedence. A common trap is changing the contents of a released version: any modification requires a new version.
mustKnow.code:
1.4.2 -> 1.4.3   Bug fix (PATCH)
1.4.3 -> 1.5.0   New functionality (MINOR); PATCH resets
1.5.0 -> 2.0.0   Remove an API in use (MAJOR); MINOR and PATCH reset

1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0

mustKnow.title: Refactoring: change structure, preserve behavior
mustKnow.body: Martin Fowler defines refactoring as changing software’s internal structure to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing observable behavior. Its core is a series of small steps that preserve behavior, making mistakes less likely and keeping the system fully working after every step. In practice, automated tests should verify unchanged behavior; this is a general practice, not a statement from Fowler’s definition page. Refactoring belongs in everyday development, such as preparing existing code for a new feature before adding it, and need not be a separate project. Common traps are calling bug fixes or feature additions “refactoring”, or restructuring without tests.

mustKnow.title: Kanban: Definition of Workflow, WIP, and SLE
mustKnow.body: The Kanban Guide (2025) defines Kanban as a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through three practices: defining and visualizing a workflow, actively managing its items, and improving it. The Definition of Workflow must include at least the definition of work items, start and finish points, workflow states, WIP control, flow policies, and a service level expectation (SLE). An SLE forecasts both time and probability, such as 85% of items finishing within eight days, based on historical cycle time. WIP counts items started but not finished, and controlling it should establish a pull system: start work when capacity becomes available. A common trap is having a multi-column board without controlling WIP or examining flow data.

mustKnow.title: Product Backlog refinement: items ready for selection
mustKnow.body: Under the Scrum Guide, items that the team can complete within one Sprint are ready for selection during Sprint Planning. Refinement usually provides this clarity by breaking down and defining items to make them smaller and more precise. It is an ongoing activity that adds detail, order, and size, described under Product Backlog rather than listed as a Scrum event. The Developers doing the work are responsible for sizing, while the Product Owner helps clarify trade-offs. Common traps are leaving large items to unpack during Sprint Planning or having others estimate on behalf of Developers.

mustKnow.title: Blameless postmortems: why did the system allow failure?
mustKnow.body: Google SRE defines a postmortem as a record of an incident, its impact, mitigation actions, causes, and follow-up work to prevent recurrence. A blameless postmortem identifies contributing causes without blaming individuals or teams, assuming everyone had good intentions and acted appropriately with the information available. Fear of punishment discourages disclosure. Rather than writing that Somchai ran the wrong script, ask why systems or procedures allowed the mistake. Define in advance which incidents require postmortems.

mustKnow.title: Design docs: goals, non-goals, and alternatives
mustKnow.body: A design doc records a high-level implementation strategy and important design decisions, emphasizing the trade-offs considered. In Malte Ubl’s Design Docs at Google, valuable sections include goals/non-goals and alternatives considered. A non-goal is not the reverse of a goal; it is something that could have been a goal but was deliberately excluded. Alternatives explain why the chosen approach best serves the goals. Docs identify design problems while changes are inexpensive, but they have a cost and are unnecessary when the solution is already clear. A document that becomes an implementation manual signals that one may not be needed; small tasks can use a one-to-three-page mini design doc.

mustKnow.title: Write changelogs for people: Keep a Changelog
mustKnow.body: A changelog records noteworthy changes for users by version in chronological order. Keep a Changelog recommends writing for humans rather than machines, including an entry for every version, grouping changes into Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, and Security, listing the latest version first, including release dates, and stating whether Semantic Versioning is used. Collect upcoming changes under Unreleased. A common trap is pasting git log into a changelog, full of noise such as merge commits and uninformative messages.
mustKnow.code:
## [Unreleased]
### Added
- Coupon field on the cart page

## [1.2.0] - 2026-09-14
### Added
- Export reports as CSV
### Deprecated
- Endpoint /v1/report will be removed in 2.0.0
### Fixed
- Incorrect total when applying two discounts

mustKnow.title: Conway’s Law: systems mirror communication structures
mustKnow.body: Melvin Conway submitted How Do Committees Invent? to Harvard Business Review, which rejected it, then to Datamation, which published it in April 1968, according to his own website. Its proposal is that organizations designing systems produce designs whose structures copy their communication structures. The same website quotes Wikipedia’s explanation that two modules cannot interface correctly unless their designers communicate; that wording is Wikipedia’s, not Conway’s. Conway’s own conclusion is that initial designs are seldom best, system concepts may need to change, and organizational flexibility matters for good design. The example of teams split by layer (UI, backend, database) producing systems where every feature requires repeated cross-team handoffs is a common interpretation, not a statement on that page.

mustKnow.title: Parallel change: expand and contract
mustKnow.body: An incompatible interface change with many consumers requires updating everyone together if made in one step, which is risky. Parallel change, or expand and contract, has three phases: expand adds the new interface while supporting old and new; migrate moves consumers individually and takes longest when they are outside the team; contract removes the old interface once nobody uses it. Fowler’s same page says most database refactorings follow parallel change, with migration as a transition between schemas until all database-accessing code has moved. The SQL below is our illustration, not Fowler’s. A common trap is stopping after expand and forgetting contract, leaving the old interface indefinitely.

mustKnow.title: Hyrum’s Law: users rely on observable behavior
mustKnow.body: Hyrum’s Law says that with enough API users, every observable system behavior will be depended on, regardless of the contract’s promises. Hyrum Wright observed it, and Titus Winters named it. This creates an implicit interface from actual usage that constrains implementation changes, such as users expecting performance levels that were never promised. Changes outside the written contract can therefore still break systems. Our practical conclusion, not a statement on the source page, is to assess consumers and communicate before changes, and not assume a PATCH version guarantees nothing will break for consumers.

questions.prompt: A story says “Managers can view sales by branch, filter dates, and export PDF/Excel”. The team estimates three Sprints. What should the first slice be?
options: Design every data warehouse table before working on other layers
A working view of yesterday’s sales by branch, without filters or export
Complete both PDF and Excel export buttons first because the request is explicit
Separate frontend and backend stories and assign them to different people
questions.explain: The first slice should be thin but usable across every layer, allowing managers to use it and give immediate feedback. Splitting by layer, such as designing the schema first or separating frontend/backend work, leaves nothing deliverable until every piece is complete.

questions.prompt: The team wrote these acceptance criteria for product search. What is the main problem?
questions.code:
Given the user is on the home page
When they enter a search term and press Enter
Then the system displays results quickly and is easy to use
options: Given should describe database state rather than the user’s location
Everything must be written in English before it can be tested
Then is not measurable, so nobody can decide whether it passes
Missing And lines prevent conversion into an automated test
questions.explain: “Quickly” and “easy to use” mean different things to different people. Make Then verifiable, such as “Show products whose names contain the search term”, and express speed as a numeric NFR such as p95 under one second. And is only an optional connector.

questions.prompt: A Product Owner writes “The system must support many users during promotions”. Which rewrite is best?
options: Support 2,000 requests per second with p95 no higher than 500 ms
Scale well as the number of users grows during promotions
Deploy on Kubernetes with autoscaling for promotional traffic
Maintain 100% availability with no downtime whatsoever
questions.explain: A good NFR specifies numbers and conditions verifiable through load testing. Kubernetes is an implementation choice rather than a requirement. A 100% target is nearly impossible and unnecessarily expensive, so targets such as 99.9% are commonly used.

questions.prompt: On the final Sprint day, an item’s code is merged but lacks tests and staging deployment required by the team’s Definition of Done. What should happen?
options: Count it as done because the code is merged; add tests in the next Sprint
Temporarily lower the DoD for this Sprint so it passes before the Review
Count half its story points so velocity reflects the work already performed
Not done: leave it out of the Increment and return it to the Product Backlog
questions.explain: Work that does not meet the DoD is not part of an Increment and cannot be presented at the Sprint Review or released (Scrum Guide 2020). Counting it as done or awarding partial points hides unfinished work and makes velocity misleading.

questions.prompt: You are reviewing a PR containing this code. Which comment helps most?
options: This does not look good; rewrite the whole section and send it again
nit: rename the variable to foundUser to match the team’s naming style
Raw URL input risks SQL injection here; use a parameterized query
SELECT * is fine for now; we can optimize it later, so I approve
questions.explain: A useful comment identifies a real problem, explains why it matters, and proposes a fix. The naming nit is not wrong but misses a much more important vulnerability. “Rewrite everything” does not explain the problem.

questions.prompt: Your lead asks whether a new payment API integration can finish by Friday. You have never used it, and its docs are incomplete. How should you respond?
options: Promise it will be ready Friday, then work overtime to meet the deadline
Estimate 5–8 business days; try the API for a day to narrow the range
Decline to estimate until coding is finished because software is unpredictable
Triple the time you expect to need, then give one definite completion date
questions.explain: An honest estimate states a range and known uncertainty, with a plan to reduce it through a short spike. Promising to please others makes everyone plan from incorrect numbers. Refusing to estimate at all does not help decisions.

questions.prompt: A pricing module has duplicated code; changes take longer and introduce bugs. The team proposes stopping features for six months to rewrite everything. Which approach fits best?
options: Track the debt and refactor frequently changed areas alongside features
Stop all feature work for six months and rewrite the entire system cleanly
Leave it alone because it still works; fix it only when there is free time
Ask the module expert to fix it secretly in spare time without telling the PO
questions.explain: Incremental repayment beginning with frequently changed areas produces faster results with lower risk while continuing to deliver value. A complete rewrite sounds clean but must recreate existing capabilities, often taking longer and carrying more risk than expected. Secret work leaves the PO prioritizing with incomplete information.

questions.prompt: A year later, a new teammate asks why PostgreSQL was chosen over MongoDB. The original decision maker has left, so the team debates it for weeks. What would best prevent this?
options: A lengthy comment explaining the decision in the database configuration file
A wiki page listing every database setting and all connection strings
A rule stating that past decisions must never be discussed again
An ADR with context, alternatives, reasons, and consequences
questions.explain: An ADR preserves why the decision was made and its original context, so newcomers can assess whether those reasons still apply. Configuration docs record only what. Forbidding reconsideration is inappropriate because changed context may justify a new ADR that supersedes the old one.

questions.prompt: During a Sprint, sales asks you to add a feature for a major customer that is not in the Sprint Backlog. What should you do?
options: Start immediately without telling anyone because a major paying customer requested it
Reject it outright because Scrum forbids all changes during a Sprint
Ask the PO to prioritize; if urgent, renegotiate scope and keep the Sprint Goal
Cancel this Sprint immediately and start a new one that includes the feature at once
questions.explain: The PO owns Product Backlog ordering, and scope can be renegotiated with the PO during a Sprint without endangering its Goal (Scrum Guide 2020). Scrum does not prohibit every change. Only the PO can cancel a Sprint, and only if its Goal becomes obsolete.

questions.prompt: The team shipped 12 features this quarter and velocity rose 30%, but checkout conversion stayed flat and customer tickets increased. What should happen next?
options: Declare success because both velocity and the number of features increased
Set a conversion outcome target and measure it after each release
Increase story point targets per Sprint so features ship even faster
Compare velocity across teams to see which team works most efficiently
questions.explain: Feature counts and velocity are outputs, not evidence of improved user or business outcomes. These numbers suggest the work may not solve the intended problem, although other factors still need examination. Measure each feature’s outcome to choose subsequent work. Story points use a team-specific scale and cannot be compared across teams.

questions.prompt: A new team says “We are Agile, so we need no documentation or planning”. Three months later, nobody can explain the system to a new teammate. Which statement best matches the Agile Manifesto?
options: The Manifesto values working software over documentation, but keeps what is needed
The Manifesto bans documentation and planning because they are waterfall practices
The Manifesto values both equally and requires complete documentation before coding
The Manifesto says nothing about documentation and leaves it entirely to company custom
questions.explain: The Manifesto says the items on the right, including documentation, have value but values those on the left more. This expresses relative weight, not a ban. Both forbidding docs and requiring complete docs before coding go beyond its wording.

questions.prompt: A department manager asks the Scrum Master to assign each person a story during Sprint Planning. Under the Scrum Guide, who decides how to divide and perform the work?
options: The Product Owner, because responsibility for value includes assigning who does what and when
The Developers, because turning Product Backlog items into an Increment is at their discretion
The Scrum Master, because responsibility for effectiveness includes assigning work by ability
The department manager, because organizational authority permits individual assignments
questions.explain: The Scrum Guide says how Developers turn items into an Increment is their own discretion; nobody tells them how. The Scrum Master is accountable for establishing Scrum and team effectiveness, not assigning individual tasks.

questions.prompt: The organization’s Definition of Done requires code review and tests. Team A wants its own DoD without review to ship faster. Is this allowed under the Scrum Guide?
options: Yes, the team owns its DoD, so it may remove criteria if the PO accepts the risk
Yes, if the Scrum Master records a time-limited exception in the Sprint Backlog
No, an organizational DoD is a minimum; teams may add criteria but not remove them
Only in Sprints near a deadline, with reviews completed afterward when time allows
questions.explain: When the DoD is part of organizational standards, every Scrum Team must follow it as a minimum. A team can be stricter but cannot reduce the criteria, even with PO or Scrum Master agreement.

questions.prompt: Three consecutive Sprint Retrospectives produced long lists of agreed problems, yet nothing changed in the next Sprint. Under the Scrum Guide, how should the team improve?
options: Send all problems to management because the team cannot change how it works
Hold only two Retrospectives per year and fix all accumulated problems together
Let the Scrum Master fix everything during the Sprint without team involvement
Choose a few high-impact improvements and put them in the next Sprint Backlog
questions.explain: The Scrum Team identifies the most helpful changes; the most impactful improvements should be addressed promptly and may enter the next Sprint Backlog. Retrospectives occur at the end of every Sprint. They are not work to hand off to management or the Scrum Master, who helps the team improve its own practices.

questions.prompt: An internal library is at 2.3.1. The team deprecates oldFormat() in favor of format(), without removing it or changing behavior. What is the next Semantic Version?
questions.explain: The specification requires MINOR to increase when public API functionality is marked deprecated, resetting PATCH to zero: 2.4.0. Although behavior is unchanged, PATCH applies to bug fixes. 3.0.0 applies when the function is actually removed.

questions.prompt: After deprecating oldFormat() in 2.4.0, the team removes it from the public API while keeping format(). Which version should be released?
questions.explain: Removing a public API function is incompatible, requiring a MAJOR increase and resetting MINOR and PATCH to zero: 3.0.0. Prior deprecation gives consumers time to migrate but does not make removal compatible.

questions.prompt: The library’s listTags() never documented result order but returned insertion order. A new version deduplicates and sorts alphabetically. The contract is unchanged, yet consumers report breakage. What is the best conclusion?
options: Consumers relied on an undocumented order, so the library bears no responsibility
The unchanged public API makes this a valid PATCH with no impact on consumers
Hyrum’s Law: users depend on observable behavior even without a promise
Only consumers should fix it; providers need not consider undocumented usage
questions.explain: Hyrum’s Law says observable behavior can acquire dependents even when the contract does not promise it. Blaming consumers may fit the contract but does not prevent outages. Calling the PATCH safe ignores the implicit interface.

questions.prompt: An automated release tool follows Conventional Commits to choose versions. What version increase does the commit below imply?
questions.code:
fix: lowercase email before lookup

BREAKING CHANGE: Emails containing uppercase letters will no longer match existing accounts
options: PATCH, because the fix type always corresponds to a patch release
MINOR, because this changes the behavior of an existing feature
No release, because fix does not count as a new feature
MAJOR, because BREAKING CHANGE applies to any commit type
questions.explain: The specification says a BREAKING CHANGE footer, or ! after the type/scope, denotes a breaking API change associated with MAJOR, for any commit type. PATCH seems plausible from fix but ignores the footer’s effect on the entire commit.

questions.prompt: A 300-line commission module has no tests. The team wants clearer structure before adding a rule. What is the best first refactoring step?
options: Add tests for current behavior, then refactor in small, tested steps
Rewrite the module in one go, then compare results manually at week’s end
Fix bugs while restructuring to avoid multiple PRs and repeated changes
Add the rule in the existing code, then restructure if time remains
questions.explain: Refactoring uses small behavior-preserving steps with a working system after each. Tests capturing existing behavior provide a practical safety net; Google eng-practices also expects pure refactoring CLs to have coverage or add it. Whole-module rewrites or mixed bug fixes make behavior changes hard to distinguish.

questions.prompt: A four-person team has 14 in-progress items, all stuck for days with almost nothing finishing. What should Kanban improve first?
options: Add more detailed board columns to show the status of every work item
Control WIP and pull new work only when capacity is available
Have everyone work on more items at once to clear the backlog faster
Pull more work onto the board to make the throughput number look higher
questions.explain: The Kanban Guide requires defining WIP control for started but unfinished items and pulling work when capacity exists. Little’s Law, separately from the Guide, explains that with stable throughput, more concurrent unfinished items increase average cycle time. More columns improve visibility without addressing the cause.

questions.prompt: A manager reads an SLE of “85% of items finish within eight days” and assumes every item will. Which interpretation is correct?
options: Every item must finish in eight days or someone must be held accountable
It is the average duration, so half the items always finish within eight days
It is a time-and-probability forecast based on the team’s historical cycle time
It is an unchangeable customer contract requiring SLA renegotiation when exceeded
questions.explain: The Kanban Guide says SLE combines a time period and a probability, based on historical cycle time. Around 15% of items may therefore exceed eight days. It is neither an average nor a promise; it helps manage aging work.

questions.prompt: A Product Owner adds “improve the entire reporting system” as one three-month Product Backlog item. The team cannot select it during Sprint Planning. What should have happened earlier?
options: The PO should estimate it and require Developers to accept the number
Wait for Sprint Planning to break it down in a single meeting
The Scrum Master should break it down without consulting Developers
Refine continuously into items doable in one Sprint, sized by Developers
questions.explain: The Guide considers items ready when they can finish within one Sprint. Refinement is ongoing, with Developers responsible for sizing. Leaving all decomposition for Planning makes it long and unclear. PO or Scrum Master sizing on behalf of Developers conflicts with the Guide.

questions.prompt: A CSV export meets the DoD on day three of a two-week Sprint. Customers want it now, but a manager requires waiting for the final Sprint Review demo. What does the Scrum Guide say?
options: It can be released earlier; Sprint Review is not a release gate
It must wait for the Review so stakeholders can authorize release
It cannot ship before Sprint end because an Increment exists only then
It may be released only with written Scrum Master approval
questions.explain: The Guide says an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders before Sprint end, and Sprint Review should not be a release gate. An Increment exists as soon as an item meets the DoD.

questions.prompt: A developer writes an eight-page design doc for adding an alternate phone field to a profile form. It lists line-by-line file changes with no alternatives. How does Design Docs at Google suggest viewing this?
options: Good: line-level detail helps reviewers and avoids follow-up questions
Unnecessary: implement the clear solution and explain it in the PR
Incomplete: add non-goals and it will be sufficient for design review
Too short: it needs 10–20 pages to qualify as a good design doc
questions.explain: The article treats design docs as a cost, useful when solutions are unclear. An implementation manual suggests one may be unnecessary. Small work can use one-to-three-page mini docs. Adding non-goals or more length misses that this problem may not need a doc at all.

questions.prompt: A checkout outage postmortem says “Root cause: Somchai ran a migration against the wrong production database”. Which rewrite best fits blameless practice?
options: Replace the name with “an engineer” but still blame their lack of care
Hide the script details and describe only “a temporary system problem”
Record what happened, ask why procedures allowed it, and fix the system
Keep the name, add an apology, and send Somchai for production training
questions.explain: Blameless postmortems assume good intentions and ask why systems or processes allowed a mistake, then improve them. Anonymizing blame is still blame, while hiding facts prevents learning.

questions.prompt: Teams are divided into Frontend, Backend, and Database. Leadership wants business services such as Payment and Catalog, yet every feature still requires three handoffs a year later. What best fits Conway’s Law?
options: Train everyone in microservices and domain-driven design to improve their skills
Improve CI/CD tooling to support many services deployed independently
Require every team to use the same language to unify the system’s structure
Systems mirror communication; align teams with business boundaries
questions.explain: Conway’s Law says system design copies organizational communication structures. Layer-based teams tend to create work spanning several teams; aligning teams with desired boundaries is a common application. Conway himself emphasized organizational flexibility for good design. Training and tools alone do not fix the underlying structure.

questions.prompt: Five independently deployed services read users.phone. The team wants to rename the column to mobile without breaking any service and proposes the migration below. What is safer under parallel change?
questions.code: ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN phone TO mobile;
options: Add mobile, write both columns, migrate services, then drop unused phone
Keep RENAME and ask every team to deploy immediately after the migration
Run RENAME at night and deploy all five services within the same window
Add only mobile and retain phone forever because removing it is too risky
questions.explain: Parallel change separates expand, migrate, and contract. Before contract, each step can deploy while old services still work; phone is removed only when unused. A one-step RENAME requires simultaneous migration. Never removing phone skips contract and leaves old structures indefinitely.

questions.prompt: A 2,400-line PR combines structural refactoring, a new feature, and a bug fix. Two reviewers approve without careful reading. Under Google’s eng-practices guidance, what should the team do?
options: Require reviewers to spend half a day reading the entire change
Split it into several self-contained, single-purpose PRs with their own tests
Merge first and let QA review instead to meet the deadline
Compress code to reduce lines while keeping all three changes together
questions.explain: Google recommends small, single-purpose changes because they receive faster, deeper reviews, contain fewer bugs, and are easier to roll back. Tests should accompany their changes. Relying on QA or compressing lines does not improve reviewer comprehension.

questions.prompt: A reviewer has blocked a PR that clearly improves readability for three days over three preferred variable names. What does Google’s review standard suggest?
options: Block until all three preferences are met because reviewers should demand perfection
Approve without any comments because every reviewer comment delays the PR
Approve the code-health improvement; mark naming preferences optional
Ask another reviewer to decide without answering the author’s naming questions
questions.explain: Google favors approving changes that definitely improve code health even when imperfect: there is better code, not perfect code. Style outside a style guide is personal preference. Reviewers may comment, but minor polish that should not block can begin with “Nit:”; comments.html defines Nit as a technically worthwhile but low-impact point, while truly optional suggestions use Optional or Consider. Blocking for perfection slows improvement and discourages useful changes.

questions.prompt: After releasing 1.2.0, the team creates CHANGELOG.md by pasting all git log --oneline output. Library users cannot understand it. What does Keep a Changelog suggest?
questions.code:
a1f3c9e Merge branch 'feat/csv'
7b02d41 wip
c93e5aa fix typo in docs
e4410bd csv export
options: Add a header telling users to read the complete repository commit log
Reverse the commit order and remove merges, leaving everything else
Format the log attractively and include the author of every commit
Select key changes, group Added/Fixed, and include the release date
questions.explain: Keep a Changelog says changelogs are for humans, not machines. Commit logs include noise such as merges and unclear messages, so entries should be selected, edited, and grouped. Formatting or reversing the same noisy log does not fix its content.

exercises.title: Write a user story and acceptance criteria
exercises.prompt: A customer requests: “Notify me when a product I want is back in stock”. Write one user story, at least two Given / When / Then acceptance criteria (preferably including at least one case outside the happy path), and at least one non-functional requirement with a measurable number and unit.
exercises.context: An online shop already has inventory tracking and an email service. Popular products sell out quickly, and many customers are waiting to buy.
exercises.starter:
## User story
As a ...

## Acceptance criteria

## Non-functional
exercises.solution:
## User story
As a customer waiting for an out-of-stock product,
I want to subscribe to back-in-stock notifications
so that I can buy it before it sells out again.

## Acceptance criteria
1. Given a product is out of stock
   When the customer selects “Notify me”
   Then the system records the request and displays a confirmation
2. Given a customer has subscribed to notifications
   When the product's stock rises above 0
   Then the system sends the customer exactly one notification email
3. Given a customer has already subscribed to notifications
   When they select “Notify me” again
   Then the system creates no duplicate request and says they are already subscribed

## Non-functional
- Send at least 10,000 notification emails per hour
- Send notifications within 15 minutes of restocking at p95
hints: Start with “As a <user>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>”.
Separate the customer subscribing from the product returning to stock. Consider repeated clicks or the product selling out again.
An NFR needs a number and unit, such as within 15 minutes at p95 or 10,000 emails per hour.

checks.pattern: ในฐานะ\s*[ก-๙a-z]|as an? [a-z]

checks.label: State the desired capability
checks.pattern: ต้องการ|อยาก|i want|i'd like|i would like

checks.label: Include a numeric non-functional requirement with a unit
checks.pattern: (non-?\s?functional|nfr|ไม่ใช่ฟังก์ชัน|ด้านคุณภาพ|quality attributes?)[\s\S]*\d[\d,.]*\s*(?:\w+\s+)?(ms|มิลลิวินาที|วินาที|นาที|ชั่วโมง|วัน|%|ฉบับ|ครั้ง|คำขอ|ข้อความ|รายการ|คน|requests?|rps|seconds?|minutes?|hours?|emails?|users?|messages?|items?|(?:s|sec|secs|min|mins|h|hr|hrs)(?![a-z]))

exercises.title: Write a blameless postmortem from incident notes
exercises.prompt: Using the incident notes below, write a blameless postmortem with Summary, Impact (including numbers), Timeline (at least three timestamps), Contributing factors (systems and procedures), What went well, and Action items (each with a responsible role and due date). Do not use personal names in the document; use roles such as “the deploying engineer”.
exercises.context:
Raw notes from a fictional incident on Friday, September 25, 2026

14:02 Somchai (backend developer) deployed a new payment-service configuration to production. The payment gateway timeout changed from 30 seconds to 3 seconds. Staging used an instantly responding mock gateway, so the issue was not visible.
14:09 Checkout error rate rose from 0.5% to 38%.
14:21 Malee (on-call) learned from support that customers could not pay. No automatic alert fired because its threshold was 50% errors sustained for 15 minutes.
14:48 The team connected the incident to the latest configuration and began rollback.
14:55 Error rate returned to normal.

Impact: 1,240 failed orders; 87 customers were charged without an order and needed refunds.
Additional information: configuration changes require no code review and there is no canary.
exercises.starter:
# Postmortem: checkout outage

## Summary

## Impact

## Timeline

## Contributing factors

## What went well

## Action items
exercises.solution:
# Postmortem: checkout outage after a configuration deployment

## Summary
On Friday, September 25, 2026, at 14:02, a configuration deployment reduced the payment gateway timeout from 30 seconds to 3 seconds. Checkout errors rose to 38% for 46 minutes (14:09 to 14:55), returning to normal after rollback.

## Impact
- 1,240 failed orders
- 87 customers charged without an order; refunds required
- Detection took 12 minutes after errors began rising and did not come from an automatic alert

## Timeline
- 14:02 The deploying engineer released a new payment-service configuration
- 14:09 Checkout error rate rose from 0.5% to 38%
- 14:21 On-call learned of the issue from support (no alert fired)
- 14:48 The team linked the incident to the latest configuration and began rollback
- 14:55 Error rate returned to normal

## Contributing factors
- Staging used an instantly responding mock gateway, hiding that a 3-second timeout was too short for the real gateway
- Configuration changes could reach production without code review or a canary
- The alert threshold required 50% errors for 15 minutes, so it did not fire at 38%

## What went well
- After learning of the issue, the team identified the cause and rolled back within about half an hour
- Support reached on-call, and rollback restored the normal error rate

## Action items
| Action | Owner | Due date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Require review for production configuration changes | Platform team lead | 2026-10-16 |
| Alert on an error rate above 5% sustained for 5 minutes | On-call lead | 2026-10-09 |
| Test staging against the real gateway sandbox or add timeout tests | QA team lead | 2026-10-23 |
| Add a canary for payment-service deployments | Platform team lead | 2026-10-30 |
hints: Start with the section headings and fill them with facts from the notes. Numbers and timestamps must match.
Ask why procedures or systems allowed the mistake rather than who was at fault. Use roles such as deploying engineer or on-call instead of names.
Good action items improve systems and include an owner and due date: adjust alert thresholds, require configuration reviews, or add a canary.

checks.label: Include a What went well section
Include at least three timestamps in Timeline
Include Contributing factors or a causes section
Assign owners to Action items
Assign due dates to Action items

exercises.title: Write a commit-msg hook enforcing Conventional Commits
exercises.prompt: The team uses Conventional Commits and wants Git to reject invalid messages. Write a shell script for the commit-msg hook that: (1) reads the first line of the commit message file passed as the first argument, skipping lines beginning with #; (2) requires type(scope)!: description, with optional scope and !, a space after :, and a nonempty description; (3) accepts feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore, revert as case-insensitive types (a team convention, not a specification requirement); (4) allows Git-generated messages beginning with “Merge ” and “Revert ”; (5) prints an explanation and example to stderr and exits with code 1 on failure.
exercises.context:
Git calls commit-msg with one parameter: the path to the commit message file. A nonzero hook exit code cancels the commit; git merge also calls this hook. Save it as .git/hooks/commit-msg and run chmod +x. POSIX sh and grep -E are sufficient.

Must pass: feat: add coupon field | fix(cart)!: change rounding | Merge branch 'x'
Must fail: added stuff | feat:missing space | feature: wrong type
exercises.starter:
#!/bin/sh
# .git/hooks/commit-msg
msg_file="$1"

# TODO: validate the first line of the commit message
exercises.solution:
#!/bin/sh
# commit-msg hook: enforce Conventional Commits format
msg_file="$1"
subject=$(grep -v '^#' "$msg_file" | head -n 1)

# allow Git-generated merge and revert commits
case "$subject" in
  "Merge "*|"Revert "*) exit 0 ;;
esac

pattern='^(feat|fix|docs|style|refactor|perf|test|build|ci|chore|revert)(\([^()]+\))?!?: .*[^[:space:]]'
if ! printf '%s\n' "$subject" | grep -Eiq "$pattern"; then
  echo "Invalid commit message format: <type>(<scope>)!: <description>" >&2
  echo "Example: feat(api)!: remove endpoint v1" >&2
  exit 1
fi
hints: Git passes the file path as $1. Use grep -v or sed to read the first non-comment line into a variable.
Build an extended regex such as ^(type1|type2|...)(\(scope\))?!?: .+ and test it with grep -Eiq. Handle Merge and Revert first using case.
On a mismatch, echo the explanation to stderr with >&2 and exit 1. Otherwise allow a successful exit (0). Return exit 0 for Merge and Revert at the beginning.

checks.label: Read the message file from the first argument ($1)
Check at least feat and fix types
Support optional ! for a breaking change

cheatsheet: Agile completes the SDLC in short iterations to get feedback on working software.
A user story uses “As a… I want… so that…”; “so that” identifies the actual problem, and the story starts a conversation.
Given is the starting state, When the action, and Then a verifiable result; acceptance criteria must also cover failure cases.
Functional requirements say what the system does; NFRs say how well it must do it and must be verifiable.
DoD is the team’s shared quality standard; acceptance criteria are specific to each story.
Code review focuses on correctness, security, design, and tests; leave style to formatters or linters.
SemVer: MAJOR for incompatible public API changes, MINOR for compatible feature additions, PATCH for compatible bug fixes.
Refactoring changes structure without changing observable behavior; use small steps and automated tests to verify it.
An estimate is a prediction, not a promise; give a range with assumptions and risks, and use a time-boxed spike for unknowns.
Parallel change: expand supports old and new, migrate moves consumers individually, contract removes the old interface once unused.
